opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is the feedback signal. The way these models get really good at something now is through reinforcement learning on top of pre-training, and RL works best when you can cheaply and reliably check whether an answer is right. In math, you can check whether the final answer matches, or with formal proofs whether the proof goes through. In programming, you can run the code against unit tests. That gives you millions of clean reward signals, and the model can iterate and improve against them very efficiently.

Research ideas are a different story. Whether an idea is good often isn't clear for months or years. You have to run the experiments, see whether it generalizes, see whether other people build on it. The signal is sparse, delayed, noisy, and often subjective. Even human experts disagree a lot about which ideas are promising. So you just can't run that tight training loop, and you don't get the same rapid progress.

There's also a data issue. The internet is full of worked solutions to math problems and code. It's much thinner on the actual process of coming up with a good research direction: the dead ends, the taste, the judgment calls about what's worth pursuing. Much of that is tacit knowledge that lives in people's heads or in lab conversations, not in text.

I'd also add some caution about how impressive the math and coding results really are. A lot of benchmark tasks are self-contained and well-specified, unlike real work, where much of the difficulty is figuring out what the problem even is, dealing with messy context, and working over long time horizons. So part of the gap you're describing isn't really math versus research. It's well-specified, short-horizon, verifiable tasks versus open-ended, long-horizon, hard-to-evaluate ones. My expectation is that progress on the latter will come, but more slowly, and it will probably require either better ways of generating feedback or models that learn much more like humans do, from real-world deployment and experience rather than curated reward signals.

r001.rationale: The response says easy verification provides clean reinforcement-learning reward signals and notes abundant worked solutions, but it does not state that easy verification makes high-quality synthetic data easier to generate.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest explanation is that it's a training data and reward signal story. When you have a task with a clean, cheap verifier, like a unit test passing or a numerical answer matching, you can run reinforcement learning at enormous scale. You generate millions of attempts, you grade them automatically, and you reinforce whatever worked. That's a very efficient loop, and the labs have poured a lot of compute into it over the last couple of years, which is why we've seen such rapid gains on competition math and on coding benchmarks.

Research ideas are almost the opposite kind of task. The feedback is slow, expensive, and noisy. To know whether an idea was good, someone often has to actually go and do the experiment, which might take weeks or months, and even then the signal is confounded by execution quality and luck. So you can't easily build the same kind of automated reward signal, and the models end up relying much more on what they picked up from pretraining, which is the written record of ideas that already exist rather than the process of generating new ones.

There's also a selection effect in what gets written down. Papers describe the idea that worked, cleaned up after the fact. They very rarely describe the hundred bad ideas that got discarded, or the tacit judgment about which directions are promising. That judgment is exactly what you'd want the model to learn, and it's mostly absent from the training distribution.

So I don't think this reflects some deep limit on what these systems can do. It reflects where it's been easy to get a training signal. My expectation is that as labs figure out how to construct longer-horizon environments, where the model proposes something, runs the experiment, and gets graded on the outcome, we'll see the gap narrow. It'll be slower and more compute-intensive than the math and coding progress was, but I'd be surprised if research taste turned out to be fundamentally unlearnable.

r001.rationale: It says clean, cheap verification enables generating millions of attempts, grading them automatically, and reinforcing what worked, conveying how verification supports scalable selection of high-quality generated training examples.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that verification gives you a way to turn an attempted solution into a training signal. With programming, you can run the code and see whether it passes the tests. With some mathematical problems, you can check the final answer or verify a proof. So you can have a model make lots of attempts and reinforce the ones that work, without needing a human to judge each one.

With research ideas, it's much harder to do that. An idea might sound compelling, but whether it's actually useful could depend on running experiments or doing several months of further work. And an idea can be original and correct without being particularly important. So the feedback is slower, more expensive, and less reliable.

That also makes progress harder to measure. If a model produces a genuinely promising research direction, we might not recognize its value immediately. Whereas if it solves a programming problem that previous models couldn't solve, that's a fairly clear improvement.

So I wouldn't necessarily interpret the gap as showing that models fundamentally can't produce useful research ideas. We've had much better mechanisms for training and measuring performance on tasks where success is easy to check.

r001.rationale: It says verification provides a training signal and enables reinforcing successful attempts, but does not clearly state that easy verification makes it easier to generate high-quality synthetic data for AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that verification gives you a way to turn more computation into better performance. In programming, you can run the code and see whether it passes tests. In math, at least in some settings, you can check whether a proof is valid. So you can generate lots of attempts, select the ones that work, and use that feedback to train the model.

With research ideas, the feedback is much harder to obtain. An idea can sound insightful and still be wrong, or be correct but not particularly useful. Finding out whether it actually advances the field might require months of experiments. And the judgment you care about isn't just, ‘Is this true?’ It's also, ‘Is this novel? Does it matter? Is it worth pursuing relative to other things we could do?’

That makes it harder both to train these systems and to measure whether they're improving. I don't think that means generating useful research ideas is necessarily beyond them. But the machinery that has worked well for math and programming depends on having a relatively cheap, reliable signal of success, and research often doesn't give you that.

r001.rationale: It explains that verification lets models generate many attempts, select successful ones, and use them for training, conveying how easy verification supports better synthetic training data.
